newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: U.S.'s Albright hails peace in Guatemala.
newsitem.headline: U.S.'s Albright hails peace in Guatemala.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright praised Guatemala on Sunday for ending its bloody 36-year civil war and promised the United States would help the country heal its Cold War wounds.

Albright's one-day visit was intended as a visible sign of U.S. support to Guatemala's fledgling era of peace after former leftist rebels and the government of President Alvaro Arzu signed a peace accord on Dec. 29.

Albright met government officials and their former battlefield adversaries as she toured a guerrilla disarmament camp in northwestern Guatemala, a symbol of peace here after a war that killed at least 100,000 people.

"You have come a long way and thanks to the peace accords you have a chance to live in peace and happiness," Albright told a crowd of several hundred peasants and former rebels gathered at the Tululche camp some 40 miles (60 km) north of Guatemala City.

The makeshift camp was one of eight in Guatemala which housed some 3,000 former members of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit in the past three months while they turned in weapons and prepared to return to society after decades of clandestine rebellion.
Albright toured the camp with former rebel Commander Randal, one of the many rebels who were the target of the U.S.-backed Guatemalan army's anti-insurgency campaign from the 1960s to the 1980s.
Befitting the occasion, Randal dressed in jeans and T-shirt instead of his old military-style garb.

The event's feel-good atmosphere belied decades of Cold War conflict in the impoverished Central American nation. After decades of funding the Guatemalan army, U.S. aid was cut off because of the army's hideous human rights record.
Albright brushed off reporters' questions about whether the United States owed Guatemala an apology for having helped fuel the civil war.
"History will be the judge of the past," she said, adding that U.S. policy was now aimed at helping the region recover from the scars of war.
The United States has promised $260 million over the next four years to help Guatemala pay for the costs of implementing the accords.

Arzu and Albright had lunch at the president's private ranch in western Guatemala after the camp visit. Arzu also espoused looking forward instead of dwelling on the past, Foreign Minister Eduardo Stein later told reporters.
"It's not healthy for Guatemala or its people to maintain an attitude that our problems are always someone else's fault," Stein quoted Arzu as telling Albright.

Albright said she and Arzu also had a frank discussion of a tough new U.S. immigration law which makes deporting illegal immigrants easier and has ignited concern in Central America that millions of illegals could return to the area and flood the already desperate job market.

Albright, herself an immigrant, said she sympathised with people who move to the U.S. for economic or political reasons and reiterated a previous promise that there would be no massive deportations of Central Americans.
"It will be done in a manner that is gradual and humane," she said, before departing Guatemala for Mexico, where President Bill Clinton is expected to arrive on Monday.
